Historical observations for this pairing come from thousands of weather stations throughout the United States, some of which have been in place for a century or more. Data have been adjusted to account for any biases that might be introduced by factors such as station moves, urbanization near the station, changes in measuring instruments, and changes in the exact times at which measurements are taken.

Model outputs are based on a set of 16 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere and how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land. These same 16 models were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 16 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

This feature uses meteorological seasons, which means spring is March–May, summer is June–August, fall is September–November, and winter is December–February. The graph shows annual anomalies, or the difference relative to the average temperature from 1901 to 2000.
